questions.prompt: There are 1000 commits between a release that works and one that does not, and each test takes a minute. Roughly how many tests does `git bisect` need to name the commit that changed the behaviour?
choices: About 500, because on average the change is in the middle
1000, because every commit has to be built once
About 10, because each test removes about half of the commits that can still be the first bad one
It depends on the number of authors, because bisect groups commits by author
questions.explanation: Each verdict clears either the tested commit's ancestors (good) or everything that is not its ancestor (bad), so the suspects halve each time: log2(1000) is about 10. Untestable commits that have to be skipped add a few more tests.

questions.prompt: The bad commit `H` and the good commit `A` have 14 candidates between them. The merge `M1` reaches 7 of them, a commit on the main line reaches 9. Which one does `git bisect` test first, and why?
choices: `M1`, because whatever the verdict, 7 candidates remain: it splits the set exactly in half
The commit that reaches 9, because it is on the main line and merges are never tested
The commit in the middle of `git log --oneline A..H`, because bisect works on the log order
`H~1`, because bisect always starts next to the bad commit
questions.explanation: Git computes for every candidate how many candidates it reaches (its weight). If it is bad, those remain; if good, the rest remain. The best test maximises the smaller of the two, which is 7 for `M1` and only 5 for a commit that reaches 9.

questions.prompt: Your `git bisect run` script exits 1 whenever `make` fails because a dependency bump broke the build for twelve commits. What happens, and what should the script do?
choices: Nothing bad: bisect ignores commits that fail to build
Bisect treats exit 1 as a crash and aborts; the script should exit 128
Bisect asks interactively whether the commit is good or bad
Those commits are marked bad, so bisect can name a commit in the broken range instead of the real one; the script should exit 125 when the build fails, so the commit is skipped
questions.explanation: For `git bisect run`, 0 means good, 125 means skip, any other code from 1 to 127 means bad, and 128 or more aborts. A build failure is not the behaviour you are looking for, so it must be reported as 125.

questions.prompt: A formatter commit reformatted the whole file, and `git blame` now shows it on every line. You add its full object name to `.git-blame-ignore-revs` and run `git blame --ignore-revs-file .git-blame-ignore-revs`. What does blame do with that commit's changes?
choices: It deletes the commit from the history before blaming
It hands each changed line to the most similar line of the parent and keeps blaming from there; a line with no similar parent line stays with the formatter commit and is marked unblamable
It shows the formatter commit's author in brackets after each line
It treats the formatter commit as a root commit, so all lines become boundary lines
questions.explanation: Ignored commits still pass unchanged lines normally; their changed lines are matched to parent lines by character-pair fingerprints. Lines that match nothing (a blank line the formatter inserted) cannot be attributed further and stay, marked `*` with `blame.markUnblamableLines`.

questions.prompt: You want the commit that introduced the constant `MAX_RETRIES = 2`. A later refactor moved that line to another place in the same file without changing it. Which command lists the introducing commit but not the refactor?
choices: `git log -G'MAX_RETRIES = 2'`, because the regex matches only real changes
`git blame` on the line, because blame always ignores moves
`git log -S'MAX_RETRIES = 2'`, because it compares the number of occurrences before and after each commit, and a move keeps the count
`git log --grep='MAX_RETRIES = 2'`, because it searches the diffs
questions.explanation: `-S` matches when the count of the string changes, so a move does not match. `-G` matches any commit whose added or removed lines match, and a move removes and adds the line. `--grep` searches commit messages, and plain blame credits the moving commit unless you pass `-M`.

questions.prompt: On Friday a teammate deleted the local branch `retry-cap` with `git branch -D`; it was never pushed. On Monday you need its last commit. Where can it still be found?
choices: In `HEAD`'s reflog (`git reflog`, "checkout: moving from retry-cap to main") and as an unreachable commit in the object database (`git fsck --no-reflogs`), in the teammate's clone, until gc expires and prunes it
In `git reflog show retry-cap`, because a branch's reflog survives the branch
On the remote, because Git pushes deleted branches to a trash folder
Nowhere: `git branch -D` deletes the commits immediately
questions.explanation: Deleting a branch removes the reference and its own reflog, not the commits. `HEAD`'s reflog still names the commits that were checked out, and the objects stay until gc prunes unreachable objects (after reflog expiry, 30 days for unreachable entries by default, and a two-week prune grace period). Nothing is on the remote if it was never pushed.
